speechtext:
I should like to proceed with the report appearing in the March issue of the Labour Gazette. It continues:
Mr. Howe said that $100,000 would be available to the company to meet initial operating expenses and that a limit of $10,000,000 had been placed upon commitments it may make without further authority.
We are providing $300,000,000 for new capital equipment, and we are planning on spending at least a billion dollars a year on production. Probably we shall have a wastage of ten per cent or $100,000,000 a year as the result of inadequate housing. This is a conservative estimate, based upon the experience of the United States during the last war.
In 1918 we found it necessary to provide $25,000,000 after having a surplus of seven to fifteen per cent in housing units at the outbreak of the war. At that time we had over 400,000 men overseas, and at this time the provision of $10,000,000 will be just a drop in the bucket in meeting Canadian needs. Hon. members will realize that during the last war small munition industries were set up in a great many small places across Canada, but the present policy seems to be to concentrate industries in large centres. I have before me a list of the industries located in Hamilton. Large numbers of people will be flocking to that city in order to find employment, and my present information is that housing is not available there. Instead of appropriating $10,000,000, I submit that this government should appropriate at least ten times that amount to provide for this acute need. My early references indicate that this expenditure would not be wasted. Housing is an asset which would be of some value during the post-war period.
With regard to the budget now before us, I am disturbed over the fact that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to change the policy in connection with the building programme. On page 2354 of Hansard he is reported as follows:
Having refrained during nearly two years of war from suggesting any discouragement to building, it has now been decided to recommend the removal of building materials from the list of exemptions under .the sales tax. In the meantime, the provision for home improvement loans has been exhausted, the application of the National Housing Act has been narrowed, and the War-time Housing Corporation has been set up to provide for the more urgent housing needs.
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson

This is not the time to curtail our building programmes, and I think the minister would be well advised to reconsider his proposal to discourage building by removing building materials from the list of exemptions. The first sentence in his statement, "having refrained during nearly two years of war from suggesting any discouragement to building", suggests that there was some doubt in his mind as to whether building should be encouraged or not. I am sure that many Canadians on reading that statement will come to the conclusion that house building should not be undertaken. I think this government should encourage in every way possible the provision of more adequate housing, especially in those congested areas where there is bound to be a wastage in our munitions industry because of lack of housing.
I think the government should provide large sums of money to carry on the building of houses manufactured from prefabricated materials. Just recently I inspected a house of this kind which had been erected in Ottawa. I am advised that this house was erected in one day by seven men who had had no previous experience in this particular field, and that the interior work was completed the next day. It is impossible to estimate the time which would be required to provide, say, 10,000 prefabricated houses.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a poor standard to go by.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Possibly it is. Prefabricated houses of this type would be a vast improvement over the majority of homes now occupied by Canadian people. After the war, such a house could be torn down, loaded on a truck and moved to another location where there was a need for it. I think the government should consider building 10,000 of these houses in strategic places. I know the old argument is often raised that you cannot very well embark on a programme of that sort without creating jealousies in other places. I think it was Doctor Samuel Johnson who once said, "Nothing will ever be attempted if all possible objections must first be overcome."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was Boswell who said that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My recollection is that it was Doctor Johnson. At any rate, I think we all agree with that sentiment. I hope this government will not wait until every objection is satisfied before it undertakes an adequate housing programme. As I said before, it is unfortunate that the responsibility for directing this most important war-time project should have been placed upon the over-worked Minister of Munitions and Supply. I believe all members will agree that the National Housing Act is one of the best pieces of legislation ever passed by this government. I think, on the whole, the department which has been directing the activities carried on under this act has done a good piece of work.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I
interject to say that it was not passed by this parliament; it was passed by two parliaments.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was
amended afterwards.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The original act did not function at all.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The original act was
passed in 1936.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was not one house constructed under the old act.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That act did not make provision for those with small incomes. The present act was passed in 1938, if I remember correctly, and according to the information I have, some 20,416 housing units have been built under the act at an expenditure of 168,619,945. The large sum of money tied up in this project may suggest to some hon. members that it has been very costly, but I imagine that if the business of this branch were wound up next year, the losses will be quite small.
In conclusion, I should like to ask hon. members to keep in mind the words uttered at noon by the Prime Minister of Australia. He said that what we need is a bigger and better and faster production of materials. He said that so far as men or the cause or the spirit were concerned, we were not inferior to the enemy. I think all hon. members will want to see the appeal made by the Prime Minister of Australia become a reality. I urge this government to consider an extensive programme of national housing as one of the essential contributions that we must make if we are going to make this a reality.
On motion of Mr. Dechene, the debate was adj ourned.

maintopic: ADDRESSES OF MR. MENZIES SUGGESTED PUBLICATION BY BUREAU OF PUBLIC INFORMATION

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ADDRESSES OF MR. MENZIES SUGGESTED PUBLICATION BY BUREAU OF PUBLIC INFORMATION
speechtext: I should like to suggest to the hon. gentleman leading the house and to the government that consideration be given to the publication by the bureau of public information of the public address made to-day by the Prime Minister of Australia before the Canadian club and, if thought wise, the address which he made to-day in this chamber. Both these speeches should receive wide distribution in Canada.

maintopic: ADDRESSES OF MR. MENZIES SUGGESTED PUBLICATION BY BUREAU OF PUBLIC INFORMATION
speechtext: I feel quite sure I can assure the leader of the opposition that his representations in that respect will be given full consideration. In fact, the suggestion had already been made that this be done.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, May 8, 1941.
